claim: Sleep disturbances negatively impact numerous functions.
source: Sleep disturbances negatively impact numerous functions and have been linked to aggression and violence.
evidence: This is a general statement about sleep disturbances that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Sleep disturbances have been linked to aggression and violence.
source: Sleep disturbances negatively impact numerous functions and have been linked to aggression and violence.
evidence: This statement references existing literature linking sleep disturbances to aggression and violence.

claim: Acute sleep deprivation profoundly suppresses aggressive behaviors in the fruit fly.
source: We find that acute sleep deprivation profoundly suppresses aggressive behaviors in the fruit fly, while other social behaviors are unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Other social behaviors are unaffected by acute sleep deprivation in the fruit fly.
source: We find that acute sleep deprivation profoundly suppresses aggressive behaviors in the fruit fly, while other social behaviors are unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing courtship behaviors remain intact after sleep deprivation.

claim: Suppression of aggression is recovered following post-deprivation sleep rebound.
source: This suppression is recovered following post-deprivation sleep rebound, and occurs regardless of the approach to achieve sleep loss.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing recovery of aggression after sleep recovery periods.

claim: Suppression of aggression occurs regardless of the approach to achieve sleep loss.
source: This suppression is recovered following post-deprivation sleep rebound, and occurs regardless of the approach to achieve sleep loss.
evidence: This is supported by data showing suppression with mechanical, thermogenetic, and temperature-dependent sleep deprivation methods.

claim: Octopamine signaling transmits changes in aggression upon sleep deprivation.
source: Genetic and pharmacologic approaches suggest octopamine signaling transmits changes in aggression upon sleep deprivation, and reduced aggression places sleep-deprived flies at a competitive disadvantage for obtaining a reproductive partner.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacologic rescue experiments with octopamine agonist CDM and genetic manipulations.

claim: Reduced aggression places sleep-deprived flies at a competitive disadvantage for obtaining a reproductive partner.
source: Genetic and pharmacologic approaches suggest octopamine signaling transmits changes in aggression upon sleep deprivation, and reduced aggression places sleep-deprived flies at a competitive disadvantage for obtaining a reproductive partner.
evidence: This is supported by competitive copulation assay data showing sleep-deprived flies win less frequently.

claim: Previous sleep experiences strongly modulate aggression with consequences for reproductive fitness.
source: These findings demonstrate an interaction between two phylogenetically conserved behaviors, and suggest that previous sleep experiences strongly modulate aggression with consequences for reproductive fitness.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing sleep deprivation affects aggression and reproductive success.

claim: Insufficient sleep impairs cognition, alertness, metabolic activity, and immune function.
source: Insufficient sleep impairs a wide range of essential processes such as cognition, alertness, metabolic activity, and immune function (Foster and Wulff, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Foster and Wulff, 2005.

claim: Sleep disruptions influence emotional processing and can modulate affective state.
source: In addition, sleep disruptions influence emotional processing and can modulate affective state (Banks and Dinges, 2007; Minkel et al., 2011, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banks and Dinges, 2007; Minkel et al., 2011, 2012.

claim: Work over many decades has suggested an interaction between sleep loss and changes in aggressive behaviors.
source: Work over many decades has suggested an interaction between sleep loss and changes in aggressive behaviors (Kamphuis et al., 2012), but even basic questions such as directionality of effect remain unresolved.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kamphuis et al., 2012.

claim: Basic questions such as directionality of effect between sleep loss and aggression remain unresolved.
source: Work over many decades has suggested an interaction between sleep loss and changes in aggressive behaviors (Kamphuis et al., 2012), but even basic questions such as directionality of effect remain unresolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citation.

claim: Chronic enforced wakefulness has been linked to increased aggression in rodents.
source: Chronic enforced wakefulness or selective REM sleep deprivation have been linked to increased aggression in rodents, although in both cases it is not possible to distinguish the potential effect of sleep loss from prolonged physical activity and/or increased stress (Kamphuis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kamphuis et al., 2012.

claim: Selective REM sleep deprivation has been linked to increased aggression in rodents.
source: Chronic enforced wakefulness or selective REM sleep deprivation have been linked to increased aggression in rodents, although in both cases it is not possible to distinguish the potential effect of sleep loss from prolonged physical activity and/or increased stress (Kamphuis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kamphuis et al., 2012.

claim: It is not possible to distinguish the potential effect of sleep loss from prolonged physical activity and/or increased stress in rodent studies of enforced wakefulness and REM sleep deprivation.
source: Chronic enforced wakefulness or selective REM sleep deprivation have been linked to increased aggression in rodents, although in both cases it is not possible to distinguish the potential effect of sleep loss from prolonged physical activity and/or increased stress (Kamphuis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the limitations of rodent studies, supported by citation.

claim: In humans, measures of irritability increase with insufficient sleep.
source: In contrast, work in humans indicates that while measures of irritability increase with insufficient sleep, aggression itself is unaffected or reduced (Kamphuis et al., 2012; Cote et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kamphuis et al., 2012; Cote et al., 2013.

claim: In humans, aggression itself is unaffected or reduced with insufficient sleep.
source: In contrast, work in humans indicates that while measures of irritability increase with insufficient sleep, aggression itself is unaffected or reduced (Kamphuis et al., 2012; Cote et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kamphuis et al., 2012; Cote et al., 2013.

claim: Human aggression can provide a competitive advantage and thereby promote survival.
source: While human aggression often carries a negative connotation, it can provide a competitive advantage and thereby promote survival.
evidence: This is a general statement about the adaptive function of aggression based on established knowledge.

claim: Dysregulated aggression and violence are significant public health concerns.
source: However, dysregulated aggression and violence are significant public health concerns (Anderson, 2012), as is chronic sleep insufficiency (Czeisler, 2013), emphasizing the need to understand how these two processes affect one another.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anderson, 2012.

claim: Chronic sleep insufficiency is a significant public health concern.
source: However, dysregulated aggression and violence are significant public health concerns (Anderson, 2012), as is chronic sleep insufficiency (Czeisler, 2013), emphasizing the need to understand how these two processes affect one another.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Czeisler, 2013.

claim: Both sleep and aggression are conserved across phylogeny.
source: Both sleep and aggression are conserved across phylogeny.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about evolutionary conservation.

claim: Drosophila has been established as a powerful model system for deconstructing the cellular and molecular basis of aggression.
source: Drosophila has been established as a powerful model system for deconstructing the cellular and molecular basis of aggression, yielding novel insights into the neural basis of fighting behaviors (Chen et al., 2002; Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2002; Asahina et al., 2014.

claim: Drosophila research has yielded novel insights into the neural basis of fighting behaviors.
source: Drosophila has been established as a powerful model system for deconstructing the cellular and molecular basis of aggression, yielding novel insights into the neural basis of fighting behaviors (Chen et al., 2002; Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2002; Asahina et al., 2014.

claim: Flies exhibit sleep-like states.
source: Flies also exhibit sleep-like states (Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000) and, in response to sleep deprivation, demonstrate deficits in behaviors like learning and memory (Seugnet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000.

claim: In response to sleep deprivation, flies demonstrate deficits in behaviors like learning and memory.
source: Flies also exhibit sleep-like states (Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000) and, in response to sleep deprivation, demonstrate deficits in behaviors like learning and memory (Seugnet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seugnet et al., 2008.

claim: Octopamine is the insect analog of norepinephrine.
source: Monoamines such as octopamine (Crocker et al., 2010), which is the insect analog of norepinephrine, and dopamine are potent regulators of arousal in Drosophila (Andretic et al., 2005; Kume et al., 2005; Lebestky et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: Octopamine and dopamine are potent regulators of arousal in Drosophila.
source: Monoamines such as octopamine (Crocker et al., 2010), which is the insect analog of norepinephrine, and dopamine are potent regulators of arousal in Drosophila (Andretic et al., 2005; Kume et al., 2005; Lebestky et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crocker et al., 2010; Andretic et al., 2005; Kume et al., 2005; Lebestky et al., 2009.

claim: Distinct subpopulations of octopamine and dopamine neurons independently modulate sleep and aggression.
source: Distinct subpopulations of neurons of each type appear to independently modulate sleep and aggression.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent detailed descriptions of specific neuronal populations and their functions.

claim: ASM neurons in the medial protocerebrum govern wake-promoting effects of octopamine.
source: For octopamine, ASM neurons in the medial protocerebrum govern wake-promoting effects (Crocker et al., 2010), while VUM cells in the anterior or posterior brain control social behavioral choice (Certel et al., 2010, 2007) or fighting behaviors (Zhou et al., 2008), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crocker et al., 2010.

claim: VUM cells in the anterior brain control social behavioral choice.
source: For octopamine, ASM neurons in the medial protocerebrum govern wake-promoting effects (Crocker et al., 2010), while VUM cells in the anterior or posterior brain control social behavioral choice (Certel et al., 2010, 2007) or fighting behaviors (Zhou et al., 2008), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Certel et al., 2010, 2007.

claim: VUM cells in the posterior brain control fighting behaviors.
source: For octopamine, ASM neurons in the medial protocerebrum govern wake-promoting effects (Crocker et al., 2010), while VUM cells in the anterior or posterior brain control social behavioral choice (Certel et al., 2010, 2007) or fighting behaviors (Zhou et al., 2008), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2008.

claim: Dopamine neurons projecting to the dorsal fan-shaped body control sleep.
source: Regarding dopamine, neurons projecting to the dorsal fan-shaped body control sleep (Ueno et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012), and a number of distinct clusters modulate aggression, including PPM3 and T1 neurons (Alekseyenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ueno et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012.

claim: A number of distinct dopamine clusters modulate aggression, including PPM3 and T1 neurons.
source: Regarding dopamine, neurons projecting to the dorsal fan-shaped body control sleep (Ueno et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012), and a number of distinct clusters modulate aggression, including PPM3 and T1 neurons (Alekseyenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alekseyenko et al., 2013.

claim: Octopamine and dopamine signaling systems are well positioned to integrate information regarding internal state and environmental demand to optimize behavioral output.
source: In sum, both of these signaling systems would be well positioned to integrate information regarding internal state and environmental demand to optimize behavioral output at a given time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the described roles of these signaling systems.

claim: Sleep serves numerous vital functions.
source: Sleep serves numerous vital functions, but aggression is also a critical behavior for acquisition of food, reproduction, and predator defense (Anderson, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Aggression is a critical behavior for acquisition of food, reproduction, and predator defense.
source: Sleep serves numerous vital functions, but aggression is also a critical behavior for acquisition of food, reproduction, and predator defense (Anderson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anderson, 2012.

claim: Disrupting sleep processes might impair the function of neuronal controls underlying aggression.
source: Disrupting sleep processes might impair the function of neuronal controls underlying aggression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential mechanism.

claim: Acute sleep deprivation resulted in a profound suppression of aggression in both within-condition and between-condition assays.
source: We found that acute sleep deprivation resulted in a profound suppression of aggression in both cases (Figure 1A; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In assays between deprived and non-deprived flies, non-deprived flies showed frequent lunges and were nearly always dominant over deprived flies.
source: In assays between deprived and non-deprived flies, non-deprived flies showed frequent lunges and were nearly always dominant over deprived flies (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Flies that were sleep deprived overnight rarely lunged, even when attacked by a non-deprived fly.
source: In contrast, flies that were sleep deprived overnight rarely lunged, even when attacked by a non-deprived fly, suggesting suppression of reactive aggression by sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Sleep deprivation suppresses reactive aggression.
source: In contrast, flies that were sleep deprived overnight rarely lunged, even when attacked by a non-deprived fly, suggesting suppression of reactive aggression by sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sleep-deprived flies rarely lunged even when attacked.

claim: In assays between 2 sleep-deprived flies, the males engaged in aggressive behaviors significantly less often than pairs of control flies.
source: In assays between 2 sleep-deprived flies, the males engaged in aggressive behaviors significantly less often than pairs of control flies (Figure 1A; Videos 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Videos 1, 2.

claim: The reduced aggression within condition did not simply derive from lack of social encounters.
source: The reduced aggression within condition did not simply derive from lack of social encounters, as sleep-deprived and control pairs spent similar amounts of time interacting during the beginning of the assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1); sleep-deprived flies could also be observed throughout the assay in close proximity without engaging in fighting behaviors, which rarely occurred in control flies.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sleep-deprived and control pairs spent similar amounts of time interacting during the beginning of the assay.
source: The reduced aggression within condition did not simply derive from lack of social encounters, as sleep-deprived and control pairs spent similar amounts of time interacting during the beginning of the assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1); sleep-deprived flies could also be observed throughout the assay in close proximity without engaging in fighting behaviors, which rarely occurred in control flies.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The latency to first lunge in pairs of sleep-deprived flies following initial social encounter was markedly increased compared to control flies.
source: When lunging did occur, the latency to first lunge in pairs of sleep-deprived flies following initial social encounter was markedly increased compared to control flies (Figure 1C), and dominance was rarely established.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dominance was rarely established in pairs of sleep-deprived flies.
source: When lunging did occur, the latency to first lunge in pairs of sleep-deprived flies following initial social encounter was markedly increased compared to control flies (Figure 1C), and dominance was rarely established.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Sleep deprivation causes deficits in both proactive and reactive aggression.
source: Together, these results suggest deficits in both proactive and reactive aggression, and demonstrate that sleep deprivation negatively impacts fighting behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental observations.

claim: Sleep deprivation negatively impacts fighting behaviors.
source: Together, these results suggest deficits in both proactive and reactive aggression, and demonstrate that sleep deprivation negatively impacts fighting behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: CS males show high sleep amounts during both day (450.77 ± 77.09 min) and night (528.91 ± 109.74 min).
source: The CS males used in our experiments show high sleep amounts during both day (450.77 ± 77.09 min) and night (528.91 ± 109.74 min; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), allowing us to test day and night sleep requirements.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mechanical sleep deprivation for 11 hr during the day reduced aggression.
source: Mechanical sleep deprivation for 11 hr during the day with fighting assays performed during the final hour of the light period also reduced aggression (Figure 1A) and shifted dominance towards non-deprived flies (Figure 1B), indicating that timing of sleep loss to day or night is not critical.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mechanical sleep deprivation for 11 hr during the day shifted dominance towards non-deprived flies.
source: Mechanical sleep deprivation for 11 hr during the day with fighting assays performed during the final hour of the light period also reduced aggression (Figure 1A) and shifted dominance towards non-deprived flies (Figure 1B), indicating that timing of sleep loss to day or night is not critical.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Timing of sleep loss to day or night is not critical for suppression of aggression.
source: Mechanical sleep deprivation for 11 hr during the day with fighting assays performed during the final hour of the light period also reduced aggression (Figure 1A) and shifted dominance towards non-deprived flies (Figure 1B), indicating that timing of sleep loss to day or night is not critical.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both day and night sleep deprivation reduce aggression.

claim: 6 hr of sleep loss resulted in suppression of fighting similar to 12 hr of sleep loss.
source: Focusing on assays within condition, we found that 6 hr of sleep loss resulted in suppression of fighting (Figure 1D) similar to 12 hr of sleep loss.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sleep deprivation for the final 1 or 3 hr(s) of the night caused no reduction in fighting behavior.
source: However, sleep deprivation for the final 1 or 3 hr(s) of the night caused no reduction in fighting behavior (Figure 1D), consistent with the timeframe of sleep loss required for learning deficits in flies (Seugnet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The timeframe of sleep loss required for aggression deficits is consistent with the timeframe required for learning deficits in flies.
source: However, sleep deprivation for the final 1 or 3 hr(s) of the night caused no reduction in fighting behavior (Figure 1D), consistent with the timeframe of sleep loss required for learning deficits in flies (Seugnet et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Seugnet et al., 2008 and comparison with current data.

claim: Continuous stimulation for 6 hr during the night/day transition period did not affect subsequent fighting.
source: Continuous stimulation for 6 hr during the night/day transition period did not affect subsequent fighting (Figure 1E), indicating that sleep deprivation and not mechanical stimulation is responsible for suppression of aggression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Sleep deprivation and not mechanical stimulation is responsible for suppression of aggression.
source: Continuous stimulation for 6 hr during the night/day transition period did not affect subsequent fighting (Figure 1E), indicating that sleep deprivation and not mechanical stimulation is responsible for suppression of aggression.
evidence: This is inferred from the control experiment showing mechanical stimulation without significant sleep loss does not affect aggression.

claim: Fighting returned to baseline levels with 1 day recovery after sleep loss.
source: Fighting returned to baseline levels with 1 day recovery after sleep loss (Figure 1A), and dominance was equally likely for a previously sleep-deprived or non-deprived fly when paired against one another (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Dominance was equally likely for a previously sleep-deprived or non-deprived fly when paired against one another after 1 day recovery.
source: Fighting returned to baseline levels with 1 day recovery after sleep loss (Figure 1A), and dominance was equally likely for a previously sleep-deprived or non-deprived fly when paired against one another (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Neither sleep deprivation, nor the mechanical stimulation used to deprive, result in injury to the fly or long-lasting impairment.
source: Thus, neither sleep deprivation, nor the mechanical stimulation used to deprive, result in injury to the fly or long-lasting impairment.
evidence: This is inferred from the recovery data showing aggression returns to baseline.

claim: Following 1 and 3 hr of recovery sleep, aggression was still markedly suppressed.
source: Following 1 and 3 hr of recovery sleep, aggression was still markedly suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the recovery time course.

claim: By 6 hr after sleep deprivation, recovery of fighting behaviors was observed, with lunge counts no longer significantly reduced compared to the 6 hr control group.
source: By 6 hr we observed recovery of fighting behaviors, with lunge counts no longer significantly reduced compared to the 6 hr control group.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the recovery time course.

claim: 9 hr after the end of sleep deprivation, levels of aggression remained indistinguishable from controls.
source: 9 hr after the end of sleep deprivation, levels of aggression remained indistinguishable from controls.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the recovery time course.

claim: There are no differences in baseline aggression in control groups throughout the day.
source: Consistent with previous work (Hoyer et al., 2008), we detected no differences in baseline aggression in control groups throughout the day (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and citation to Hoyer et al., 2008.

claim: Sleep in CS males is exquisitely sensitive to high temperatures, with near total sleep loss when exposed to 31°C overnight.
source: We noted sleep in CS males to be exquisitely sensitive to high temperatures, with near total sleep loss when exposed to 31°C overnight.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Temperature-dependent sleep deprivation resulted in reduced lunging.
source: Temperature-dependent sleep deprivation also resulted in reduced lunging with aggression assays performed the following morning at 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), indicating that suppressed aggression is not specific to mechanical sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Suppressed aggression is not specific to mechanical sleep deprivation.
source: Temperature-dependent sleep deprivation also resulted in reduced lunging with aggression assays performed the following morning at 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), indicating that suppressed aggression is not specific to mechanical sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple methods of sleep deprivation suppress aggression.

claim: 12 hr of mechanical sleep deprivation during the night had no effect on courtship behavior the following morning as measured by courtship index or copulation frequency over a 10 min period.
source: Consistent with previous work (Seugnet et al., 2011; Kayser et al., 2014), 12 hr of mechanical sleep deprivation during the night had no effect on courtship behavior the following morning as measured by courtship index or copulation frequency over a 10 min period (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and citations to Seugnet et al., 2011; Kayser et al., 2014.

claim: Like learning and memory, aggression is a specific behavior that is impaired following sleep deprivation.
source: Thus, a distinct complex behavior remains intact following acute sleep loss, suggesting that like learning and memory, aggression is a specific behavior that is impaired following sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that courtship is unaffected while aggression is impaired.

claim: Activation of octopaminergic neurons using Tdc2-GAL4 and dTrpA1 resulted in near total sleep deprivation.
source: Activation of neurons using either GAL4 line resulted in near total sleep deprivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); importantly, overnight exposure to 29°C in flies lacking either the GAL4 or UAS did not impact sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), in contrast to CS males exposed to 31°C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation of dopaminergic neurons using TH-GAL4 and dTrpA1 resulted in near total sleep deprivation.
source: Activation of neurons using either GAL4 line resulted in near total sleep deprivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); importantly, overnight exposure to 29°C in flies lacking either the GAL4 or UAS did not impact sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), in contrast to CS males exposed to 31°C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overnight exposure to 29°C in flies lacking either the GAL4 or UAS did not impact sleep.
source: Activation of neurons using either GAL4 line resulted in near total sleep deprivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1); importantly, overnight exposure to 29°C in flies lacking either the GAL4 or UAS did not impact sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), in contrast to CS males exposed to 31°C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sleep deprivation by activation of Tdc2+ neurons caused a significant suppression of aggression the following day.
source: Sleep deprivation by activation of Tdc2+ or TH+ neurons caused a significant suppression of aggression the following day (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1), while genetic and temperature controls with normal prior sleep showed no such effect (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sleep deprivation by activation of TH+ neurons caused a significant suppression of aggression the following day.
source: Sleep deprivation by activation of Tdc2+ or TH+ neurons caused a significant suppression of aggression the following day (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1), while genetic and temperature controls with normal prior sleep showed no such effect (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Genetic and temperature controls with normal prior sleep showed no suppression of aggression.
source: Sleep deprivation by activation of Tdc2+ or TH+ neurons caused a significant suppression of aggression the following day (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1), while genetic and temperature controls with normal prior sleep showed no such effect (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CDM rescued aggression following sleep deprivation via activation of Tdc2+ neurons.
source: CDM, but not L-DOPA, rescued aggression following sleep deprivation via activation of Tdc2+ neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: L-DOPA did not rescue aggression following sleep deprivation via activation of Tdc2+ neurons.
source: CDM, but not L-DOPA, rescued aggression following sleep deprivation via activation of Tdc2+ neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CDM rescued aggression following sleep deprivation via activation of TH+ neurons.
source: Surprisingly, CDM also rescued aggression following sleep deprivation via activation of TH+ neurons, while L-DOPA did not (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: L-DOPA did not rescue aggression following sleep deprivation via activation of TH+ neurons.
source: Surprisingly, CDM also rescued aggression following sleep deprivation via activation of TH+ neurons, while L-DOPA did not (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CDM rescued aggression after mechanical sleep deprivation.
source: This effect is not specific to thermogenetic sleep deprivation, as CDM alone rescued aggression after mechanical sleep deprivation as well (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Aggression-relevant octopamine function is compromised downstream of sleep deprivation signals, regardless of method of sleep loss.
source: These results suggest that aggression-relevant octopamine function is compromised downstream of sleep deprivation signals, regardless of method of sleep loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that octopamine agonist rescues aggression across different sleep deprivation methods.

claim: CDM and L-DOPA showed no increase in fighting following either 1 or 3 days of drug feeding.
source: To rule out the possibility that CDM is simply a more potent inducer of fighting behaviors, we investigated the effect of both drugs on baseline aggression and found no increase in fighting following either 1 or 3 days of drug feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Social experience through group housing of flies dramatically reduces aggression.
source: Previous work has shown that social experience through group housing of flies also dramatically reduces aggression (Wang et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2008), and we examined if a shared mechanism suppresses fighting in both cases.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2008.

claim: Reduced aggression secondary to group housing was similarly rescued either by CDM or L-DOPA.
source: In contrast to sleep deprivation, reduced aggression secondary to group housing was similarly rescued either by CDM or L-DOPA (Figure 2D), indicating that the drugs can function comparably to rescue aggression depending on the method of suppression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sleep deprivation and social experience suppress aggression through distinct though potentially overlapping mechanisms.
source: Moreover, while sleep deprivation and social experience both suppress aggression, they appear to do so through distinct though potentially overlapping mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential drug rescue effects.

claim: Sleep-deprived flies were less active than non-deprived controls following thermogenetic sleep deprivation.
source: As expected, sleep-deprived flies were less active than non-deprived controls (Figure 2E), presumably due to increased homeostatic sleep drive.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both CDM and L-DOPA rescued locomotor activity back to control levels following sleep deprivation.
source: While only CDM rescued aggressive behaviors following sleep deprivation (Figure 2B), we found that both CDM and L-DOPA rescued locomotor activity back to control levels (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Motor activity is dissociated from aggression following sleep deprivation.
source: Together, these experiments dissociate motor activity from aggression following sleep deprivation, and indicate that sleep loss itself impairs aggressive behaviors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that L-DOPA rescues locomotor activity but not aggression.

claim: Sleep loss itself impairs aggressive behaviors.
source: Together, these experiments dissociate motor activity from aggression following sleep deprivation, and indicate that sleep loss itself impairs aggressive behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A group of 2–4 Tdc2+ neurons in the posterior fly brain within the VUM cluster near the suboesophageal (SOG) ganglion have been implicated in the role of octopamine modulation of aggression.
source: A group of 2–4 Tdc2+ neurons in the posterior fly brain within the VUM cluster near the suboesophageal (SOG) ganglion have been implicated in the role of octopamine modulation of aggression (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2008.

claim: These Tdc2+ Cha- neurons can be targeted genetically using Tdc2-GAL4 with the Cha-GAL80 suppressor.
source: These neurons can be targeted genetically using Tdc2-GAL4 with the Cha-GAL80 suppressor (Figure 3A; Figure 3—source data 1) (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2008 and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Activation of Tdc2+ Cha- neurons did not cause sleep deprivation.
source: Activation of Tdc2+ Cha- neurons did not cause sleep deprivation (Figure 3B), consistent with research localizing the wake-promoting octopamine neurons to dorsal brain regions (Crocker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Wake-promoting octopamine neurons are localized to dorsal brain regions.
source: Activation of Tdc2+ Cha- neurons did not cause sleep deprivation (Figure 3B), consistent with research localizing the wake-promoting octopamine neurons to dorsal brain regions (Crocker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crocker et al., 2010.

claim: Sustained activation of Tdc2+ Cha- neurons did not impair aggression the following day.
source: Importantly, sustained activation of Tdc2+ Cha- neurons also did not impair aggression the following day (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Reduced aggression following overnight activation of Tdc2+ neurons is not caused by hyperstimulation of Tdc2+ Cha- neurons.
source: Together these results show that reduced aggression following overnight activation of Tdc2+ neurons is not caused by hyperstimulation of Tdc2+ Cha- neurons, and further suggest that sleep deprivation per se is required for suppression of aggression.
evidence: This is inferred from the control experiment showing activation of Tdc2+ Cha- neurons alone does not impair aggression.

claim: Sleep deprivation per se is required for suppression of aggression.
source: Together these results show that reduced aggression following overnight activation of Tdc2+ neurons is not caused by hyperstimulation of Tdc2+ Cha- neurons, and further suggest that sleep deprivation per se is required for suppression of aggression.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that activation of aggression neurons without sleep deprivation does not impair aggression.

claim: Octopamine modulates the choice between courtship and aggression in males.
source: In addition to a role in promoting aggression, octopamine also modulates the choice between courtship and aggression in males (Certel et al., 2010, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Certel et al., 2010, 2007.

claim: A distinct subpopulation of VUM octopamine neurons that co-express the male variant of the sex determination factor Fruitless (Fru(M)) in the anterior SOG have been implicated in behavioral choice.
source: A distinct subpopulation of VUM octopamine neurons that co-express the male variant of the sex determination factor Fruitless (Fru(M)) in the anterior SOG have been implicated in this behavioral choice (Certel et al., 2010, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Certel et al., 2010, 2007.

claim: Disturbing the function of Tdc2+ Fru(M)+ neurons results in abnormal elevation of male–male courtship.
source: Previous work has shown that disturbing the function of Tdc2+ Fru(M)+ neurons results in abnormal elevation of male–male courtship, whereas near exclusive male-female courtship with intermale aggression is found under normal conditions (Certel et al., 2010, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Certel et al., 2010, 2007.

claim: Under normal conditions, near exclusive male-female courtship with intermale aggression is found.
source: Previous work has shown that disturbing the function of Tdc2+ Fru(M)+ neurons results in abnormal elevation of male–male courtship, whereas near exclusive male-female courtship with intermale aggression is found under normal conditions (Certel et al., 2010, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Certel et al., 2010, 2007.

claim: Following mechanical sleep deprivation overnight, flies overwhelmingly courted females, with no difference in the minimal time engaged in male–male courtship compared to pairs of non-deprived control males.
source: Following mechanical sleep deprivation overnight, we found that flies overwhelmingly courted females, with no difference in the minimal time engaged in male–male courtship compared to pairs of non-deprived control males (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Social behavioral choice is normal between pairs of sleep-deprived flies.
source: Thus social behavioral choice is normal between pairs of sleep-deprived flies.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sleep-deprived flies show normal courtship choice.

claim: Non-deprived flies frequently interrupted courtship activities of the other male and at times engaged in fighting behaviors away from the female.
source: Non-deprived flies were frequently observed to interrupt courtship activities of the other male, and at times, engage in fighting behaviors away from the female altogether.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: These competitive behaviors were less frequently observed between sleep-deprived males.
source: These behaviors were less frequently observed between sleep-deprived males.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In non-deprived flies, 26% of time in the assay was spent in chains or clusters.
source: We found that in non-deprived flies, 26% of time in the assay was spent in chains or clusters; this was reduced to 17.2% in pairs of sleep-deprived males (Figure 4C; Videos 3, 4), suggesting that competitive social interactions are reduced following sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In pairs of sleep-deprived males, 17.2% of time in the assay was spent in chains or clusters.
source: We found that in non-deprived flies, 26% of time in the assay was spent in chains or clusters; this was reduced to 17.2% in pairs of sleep-deprived males (Figure 4C; Videos 3, 4), suggesting that competitive social interactions are reduced following sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Competitive social interactions are reduced following sleep deprivation.
source: We found that in non-deprived flies, 26% of time in the assay was spent in chains or clusters; this was reduced to 17.2% in pairs of sleep-deprived males (Figure 4C; Videos 3, 4), suggesting that competitive social interactions are reduced following sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sleep-deprived males spend less time in competitive courtship configurations.

claim: While social behavioral choice is unaffected by sleep deprivation, impairments in aggression influence how males competitively court a female.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that while social behavioral choice is unaffected, impairments in aggression influence how males competitively court a female.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Success in aggressive interactions has been correlated with fitness for mating.
source: Success in aggressive interactions has been correlated with fitness for mating (Dow and von Schilcher, 1975) (though not in flies bred to be hyper-aggressive [Dierick and Greenspan, 2006; Penn et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dow and von Schilcher, 1975.

claim: Success in aggressive interactions has not been correlated with fitness for mating in flies bred to be hyper-aggressive.
source: Success in aggressive interactions has been correlated with fitness for mating (Dow and von Schilcher, 1975) (though not in flies bred to be hyper-aggressive [Dierick and Greenspan, 2006; Penn et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dierick and Greenspan, 2006; Penn et al., 2010.

claim: Control flies were more likely to 'win' copulation with the female compared to sleep deprived flies (∼63% vs 37%).
source: In these assays, we found that control flies were more likely to 'win' copulation with the female compared to sleep deprived flies (∼63% vs 37%; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Thermogenetic sleep deprivation via activation of Tdc2+ neurons overnight impaired next-day performance in the competitive copulation assay against a genetically identical male.
source: Thermogenetic sleep deprivation via activation of Tdc2+ neurons overnight similarly impaired next-day performance in the competitive copulation assay against a genetically identical male (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CDM restored copulation success of sleep-deprived males competing against controls.
source: Consistent with rescue of aggressive behaviors, we found that CDM restored copulation success of sleep-deprived males competing against controls, while L-DOPA had no effect (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: L-DOPA had no effect on copulation success of sleep-deprived males competing against controls.
source: Consistent with rescue of aggressive behaviors, we found that CDM restored copulation success of sleep-deprived males competing against controls, while L-DOPA had no effect (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Neither CDM nor L-DOPA had a significant effect in competitive copulation assays against controls in the absence of sleep manipulations.
source: Neither drug had a significant effect in assays against controls (no drug) in the absence of sleep manipulations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Suppression of aggression following sleep loss is deleterious when competing with a non-deprived male for a reproductive partner.
source: These results suggest that suppression of aggression following sleep loss is deleterious when competing with a non-deprived male for a reproductive partner.
evidence: This is inferred from the competitive copulation data showing sleep-deprived flies have reduced reproductive success.

claim: Sleep deprivation reduces aggression in Drosophila while other complex social behaviors are unimpaired.
source: Here we show that sleep deprivation reduces aggression in Drosophila while other complex social behaviors are unimpaired.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings supported by experimental data.

claim: The suppression of aggression is independent of the method used to induce sleep loss.
source: The suppression of aggression is independent of the method used to induce sleep loss and reversible with sufficient recovery sleep.
evidence: This is supported by data showing multiple methods of sleep deprivation suppress aggression.

claim: The suppression of aggression is reversible with sufficient recovery sleep.
source: The suppression of aggression is independent of the method used to induce sleep loss and reversible with sufficient recovery sleep.
evidence: This is supported by recovery data showing aggression returns to baseline.

claim: Octopamine plays a role in mediating reduced aggression levels following sleep loss.
source: We provide evidence that octopamine plays a role in mediating reduced aggression levels following sleep loss, and we find using competitive courtship assays that sleep deprivation places flies at a disadvantage for reproductive success due to insufficient aggression towards competing males.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacologic and genetic experiments.

claim: Sleep deprivation places flies at a disadvantage for reproductive success due to insufficient aggression towards competing males.
source: We provide evidence that octopamine plays a role in mediating reduced aggression levels following sleep loss, and we find using competitive courtship assays that sleep deprivation places flies at a disadvantage for reproductive success due to insufficient aggression towards competing males.
evidence: This is supported by competitive copulation assay data.

claim: Aggression is a specific social behavior that becomes dysregulated by sleep deprivation.
source: These results demonstrate that aggression is a specific social behavior that becomes dysregulated by sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing selective impairment of aggression.

claim: Irritability and aggression are likely dissociable in higher organisms.
source: Subjective experience in humans indicates that irritability increases with insufficient sleep, which is supported by validated measures of emotional reactivity and mood (Banks and Dinges, 2007); however, irritability and aggression are likely dissociable in higher organisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature and current findings.

claim: Tools to measure changes to aggression in humans over relatively short-time periods (hours to days) are less well-established.
source: While there are well-validated measures of aggression as a lifetime personality trait, tools to measure changes to aggression in humans over relatively short-time periods (hours to days) are less well-established, as is measuring irritability in animal models independent of overt behavioral expression.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on knowledge.

claim: Most human studies of the interaction between sleep and aggression have been correlational and utilized self-reported measures.
source: Most human studies of the interaction between sleep and aggression have been correlational and utilized self-reported measures (Kamphuis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kamphuis et al., 2012.

claim: Research supports a reduced capacity to inhibit impulsivity to negative stimuli after sleep deprivation.
source: Nonetheless, more recent human work is informative regarding dissociation of irritability and/or impulsivity from aggression itself: research supports a reduced capacity to inhibit impulsivity to negative stimuli after sleep deprivation (Anderson and Platten, 2011), while a study designed to measure reactive aggression in sleep-deprived men reported diminished aggression in response to provocation (Cote et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anderson and Platten, 2011.

claim: A study designed to measure reactive aggression in sleep-deprived men reported diminished aggression in response to provocation.
source: Nonetheless, more recent human work is informative regarding dissociation of irritability and/or impulsivity from aggression itself: research supports a reduced capacity to inhibit impulsivity to negative stimuli after sleep deprivation (Anderson and Platten, 2011), while a study designed to measure reactive aggression in sleep-deprived men reported diminished aggression in response to provocation (Cote et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cote et al., 2013.

claim: The rodent literature supports the hypothesis that sleep insufficiency leads to increased aggression.
source: The rodent literature supports the contrasting hypothesis that sleep insufficiency leads to increased aggression (Kamphuis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kamphuis et al., 2012.

claim: Differences between rodent and human findings might result from confounds such as the impact of sustained activity or stress rather than sleep deprivation per se, or REM sleep loss vs total sleep loss.
source: These differences might result from confounds such as the impact of sustained activity or stress rather than sleep deprivation per se, or REM sleep loss vs total sleep loss.
evidence: This is speculation about potential explanations for discrepancies in the literature.

claim: The central effect of sleep deprivation on aggression appears to be conserved between flies and humans.
source: Regardless, while the repertoire of emotional experience and output in humans is far more complex than in a laboratory animal, the central effect of sleep deprivation on aggression appears to be conserved between flies and humans.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of fly data with human literature.

claim: Using multiple types of sleep deprivation stimuli combined with genetic manipulations, the data suggest that the impact of sleep deprivation on aggression is causally related to sleep loss.
source: Using multiple types of sleep deprivation stimuli combined with genetic manipulations, our data suggest that the impact of sleep deprivation on aggression is causally related to sleep loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental design and results.

claim: Experimental paradigms that prevent sleep in the face of heightened sleep need are inherently stressful to an animal.
source: Nonetheless, experimental paradigms that prevent sleep in the face of heightened sleep need are inherently stressful to an animal.
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge about sleep deprivation experiments.

claim: The specificity with which aggressive social interactions are impaired as opposed to all social behaviors serves as a strong indicator that the effects observed are not simply part of a broader stress response.
source: The specificity with which aggressive social interactions are impaired as opposed to all social behaviors serves as a strong indicator that the effects we observe are not simply part of a broader stress response; moreover, other stressors are known to negatively impact courtship behaviors (Patton and Krebs, 2001; Christie et al., 2013), suggesting that courtship is not uniquely immune to stress-related impairment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the selective impairment of aggression but not courtship.

claim: Other stressors are known to negatively impact courtship behaviors.
source: The specificity with which aggressive social interactions are impaired as opposed to all social behaviors serves as a strong indicator that the effects we observe are not simply part of a broader stress response; moreover, other stressors are known to negatively impact courtship behaviors (Patton and Krebs, 2001; Christie et al., 2013), suggesting that courtship is not uniquely immune to stress-related impairment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patton and Krebs, 2001; Christie et al., 2013.

claim: Aggression in Drosophila has long been appreciated to play a role in mate selection.
source: Aggression in Drosophila has long been appreciated to play a role in mate selection (Sturtevant, 1915; Dow and von Schilcher, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sturtevant, 1915; Dow and von Schilcher, 1975.

claim: Male flies fight more in the presence of a female.
source: Male flies fight more in the presence of a female, and recent work has shown that prior exposure to a female suppresses this effect (Yuan et al., 2014); the aforementioned study focused on aggressive behaviors occurring after male flies copulate with females in the arena, suggesting that aggression may function both to obtain a reproductive partner and possibly guard that partner after mating (Yuan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yuan et al., 2014.

claim: Prior exposure to a female suppresses the effect of increased fighting in the presence of a female.
source: Male flies fight more in the presence of a female, and recent work has shown that prior exposure to a female suppresses this effect (Yuan et al., 2014); the aforementioned study focused on aggressive behaviors occurring after male flies copulate with females in the arena, suggesting that aggression may function both to obtain a reproductive partner and possibly guard that partner after mating (Yuan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yuan et al., 2014.

claim: Aggression may function both to obtain a reproductive partner and possibly guard that partner after mating.
source: Male flies fight more in the presence of a female, and recent work has shown that prior exposure to a female suppresses this effect (Yuan et al., 2014); the aforementioned study focused on aggressive behaviors occurring after male flies copulate with females in the arena, suggesting that aggression may function both to obtain a reproductive partner and possibly guard that partner after mating (Yuan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yuan et al., 2014 and involves inference about function.

claim: Male flies will successfully court a female partner in the absence of competition even in the setting of sleep deprivation.
source: Our data indicate that even in the setting of sleep deprivation, male flies will successfully court a female partner in the absence of competition.
evidence: This is supported by the courtship data showing no impairment in non-competitive settings.

claim: When competing for a female mate against a non-deprived control male, sleep deprivation impairs sexual fitness, likely due to reduced aggression towards the other male.
source: However, when competing for a female mate against a non-deprived control male, sleep deprivation impairs sexual fitness, likely due to reduced aggression towards the other male: pharmacologic restoration of aggression with an octopamine agonist likewise rescues sexual fitness.
evidence: This is supported by competitive copulation data and pharmacologic rescue experiments.

claim: Pharmacologic restoration of aggression with an octopamine agonist rescues sexual fitness.
source: However, when competing for a female mate against a non-deprived control male, sleep deprivation impairs sexual fitness, likely due to reduced aggression towards the other male: pharmacologic restoration of aggression with an octopamine agonist likewise rescues sexual fitness.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing CDM rescues competitive copulation success.

claim: Reduced performance in the competitive copulation assay occurs in males that were isolated since eclosion, eliminating the possibility that previously-established hierarchical cues are involved.
source: Importantly, reduced performance in the competitive copulation assay occurs in males that were isolated since eclosion, eliminating the possibility that previously-established hierarchical cues are involved and emphasizing the crucial role of sleep for normal function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design using isolated males.

claim: Sleep loss is required for subsequent suppressed aggression.
source: Sleep loss is required for subsequent suppressed aggression, while prolonged prior excitation of aggression-relevant neurons has no effect on fighting the following day.
evidence: This is supported by the Tdc2+ Cha- neuron activation experiments.

claim: Prolonged prior excitation of aggression-relevant neurons has no effect on fighting the following day.
source: Sleep loss is required for subsequent suppressed aggression, while prolonged prior excitation of aggression-relevant neurons has no effect on fighting the following day.
evidence: This is supported by the Tdc2+ Cha- neuron activation experiments.

claim: Neurons involved in setting aggression levels, but not male choice between courtship and aggressive behaviors, are specifically impacted by sleep deprivation.
source: Our results implicate octopaminergic signaling in this process, and suggest that neurons involved in setting aggression levels, but not male choice between courtship and aggressive behaviors, are specifically impacted: while intermale aggression is reduced with sleep deprivation, intermale courtship is not, by default, increased.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that aggression is reduced but courtship choice is normal.

claim: While intermale aggression is reduced with sleep deprivation, intermale courtship is not, by default, increased.
source: Our results implicate octopaminergic signaling in this process, and suggest that neurons involved in setting aggression levels, but not male choice between courtship and aggressive behaviors, are specifically impacted: while intermale aggression is reduced with sleep deprivation, intermale courtship is not, by default, increased.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral choice data.

claim: Norepinephrine, the mammalian analog of insect octopamine, has a critical role in aggression in vertebrates.
source: Norepinephrine, the mammalian analog of insect octopamine, has a critical role in aggression in vertebrates; noradrenergic neurons are also important regulators of sleep-wake transitions.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge.

claim: Noradrenergic neurons are important regulators of sleep-wake transitions.
source: Norepinephrine, the mammalian analog of insect octopamine, has a critical role in aggression in vertebrates; noradrenergic neurons are also important regulators of sleep-wake transitions.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge.

claim: Identification of specific cellular subpopulations whose output is altered by sleep deprivation in Drosophila will enable mapping the neural circuits that relay sleep information to aggression centers.
source: Identification of specific cellular subpopulations whose output is altered by sleep deprivation in Drosophila will enable mapping the neural circuits that relay sleep information to aggression centers, as well as investigation of the molecular signals that control deprivation-dependent changes to octopamine aggression neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions based on the current findings.

claim: The conserved cellular substrates of sleep and aggression behaviors between flies and mammals suggest findings will be of relevance to understanding the neurobiological basis of aggression and impairment after sleep loss.
source: The conserved cellular substrates of these behaviors between flies and mammals suggest such findings will be of relevance to understanding the neurobiological basis of aggression and impairment after sleep loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary conservation.

claim: Two innate behaviors—sleep and aggression—are coupled.
source: In sum, our results indicate that two innate behaviors—sleep and aggression—are coupled, and suggest that molecular signals generated by sleep deprivation might be potential targets for selective modification of aggressive behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Molecular signals generated by sleep deprivation might be potential targets for selective modification of aggressive behaviors.
source: In sum, our results indicate that two innate behaviors—sleep and aggression—are coupled, and suggest that molecular signals generated by sleep deprivation might be potential targets for selective modification of aggressive behaviors.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the findings.
